definition: The Bradley–Terry model is a probability model for the outcome of pairwise comparisons between items, teams, or objects.
details: Given a pair of items i and j drawn from some population, it estimates the probability that the pairwise comparison i > j turns out true, as where pi is a positive real-valued score assigned to individual i. The comparison i > j can be read as "i is preferred to j", "i ranks higher than j", or "i beats j", depending on the application. For example, pi might represent the skill of a team in a sports tournament and j)}"> Pr ( i > j ) {\displaystyle \Pr(i>j)} the probability that i wins a game against j. Or pi might represent the quality or desirability of a commercial product and j)}"> Pr ( i > j ) {\displaystyle \Pr(i>j)} the probability that a consumer will prefer product i over product j. The Bradley–Terry model can be used in the forward direction to predict outcomes, as described, but is more commonly used in reverse to infer the scores pi given an observed set of outcomes. In this type of application pi represents some measure of the strength or quality of i {\displaystyle i} and the model lets us estimate the strengths from a series of pairwise comparisons. In a survey of wine preferences, for instance, it might be difficult for respondents to give a complete ranking of a large set of wines, but relatively easy for them to compare sample pairs of wines and say which they feel is better. Based on a set of such pairwise comparisons, the Bradley–Terry model can then be used to derive a full ranking of the wines. Once the values of the scores pi have been calculated, the model can then also be used in the forward direction, for instance to predict the likely outcome of comparisons that have not yet actually occurred. In the wine survey example, for instance, one could calculate the probability that someone will prefer wine i {\displaystyle i} over wine j {\displaystyle j} , even if no one in the survey directly compared that particular pair.

explainer.lead: The Bradley–Terry model turns simple head-to-head choices into numerical strengths for the things being compared. It is useful when asking people to compare two options is easier than asking them to rank a whole set, and it can also predict comparisons that have not happened yet.

tiers.eli5: Imagine tasting cookies two at a time and picking your favourite each time. After enough choices, this model gives every cookie a score and puts them in order, without anyone having to rank them all at once. Those scores can also estimate which cookie someone would pick in a new pairing.
tiers.practitioner: Fit positive scores to observed pairwise outcomes, then use them to rank items or estimate the probability of an unobserved comparison. Typical applications include team skill and product-preference surveys. The scores summarize the comparisons supplied to the model; they do not by themselves explain why one item is preferred.
tiers.paperLevel: Each item i has a positive real-valued score p_i, with Pr(i > j) = p_i / (p_i + p_j). The model is commonly used in reverse to infer scores from observed pairwise outcomes, and those scores can then produce rankings or predictions for new pairs. It models pairwise preference or victory probabilities, rather than the causes of those outcomes.

explainer.example: Suppose wine i has inferred score p_i = 3 and wine j has p_j = 1. The model gives Pr(i > j) = 3 / (3 + 1) = 0.75, so it estimates a 75% chance that someone will prefer wine i, even if that particular pair was not tasted together in the survey.

usedIn.name: Sports tournaments
usedIn.detail: A team's score represents its skill, and the model estimates its probability of beating another team.

usedIn.name: Consumer product research
usedIn.detail: Product scores represent quality or desirability inferred from paired consumer preferences.

usedIn.name: Wine preference surveys
usedIn.detail: Paired tastings can be combined into a full wine ranking without requiring respondents to rank every wine.

explainer.intuition: A comparison between two items is treated as a contest between their underlying strengths. The greater an item's score relative to its opponent's, the more likely it is to be preferred or to win.
howItWorks: Collect pairwise outcomes, such as which team won or which product was preferred.
Assign every item a positive score representing its strength or quality.
Infer the scores that account for the observed set of comparisons.
Use the scores to build a full ranking or calculate probabilities for new pairings.
explainer.whyItMatters: It makes large ranking tasks manageable by replacing one difficult complete ranking with many easier pairwise choices. The same fitted scores support both an overall ranking and predictions about comparisons that have not yet occurred.
misconceptions: It is not only a prediction rule: its common use is inferring item scores from observed outcomes.
A pairwise ranking need not be collected as a complete ranking; individual comparisons can be enough to build one.
